title: Bivariate Decision Trees: Smaller, Interpretable, More Accurate

problem.claim: Univariate decision trees can be interpretable but often lack competitive predictive accuracy because they cannot model feature correlations.

gap.claim: Multivariate trees capture correlations better but can be difficult to interpret, motivating an intermediate model using two features per node.

contributions.claim: The paper advocates bivariate decision trees that use two features in each decision node.
The paper presents a fast algorithm based on CART and a slower alternating-optimization algorithm with feature regularization.
Bivariate trees are described as supporting supervised hierarchical two-dimensional visualization and construction of discriminative new features.

author_reported_evidence.claim: Bivariate trees typically produce higher accuracy than univariate trees while being much smaller.
The alternating-optimization algorithm produces the best trees while still scaling to large datasets.
The method can reveal patterns such as clusters or linear structure through supervised hierarchical two-dimensional visualization.

narrative_sequence.summary: Univariate decision trees make predictions using one feature at each node.
Their interpretability is accompanied by weaker predictive accuracy because they do not model feature correlations.
Multivariate trees model correlations more effectively but may be harder to interpret.
Bivariate trees are proposed as a middle ground using two features per node.
The paper introduces two learning algorithms and describes additional uses for feature construction and visualization.

unknowns: The abstract does not provide datasets, quantitative results, baselines, or evaluation metrics.
The abstract does not specify the algorithms' exact optimization procedures or feature-regularization formulation.
